questions.q: In what year was the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms added to the Constitution?
questions.e: The Constitution of Canada was amended in 1982 to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

questions.q: With which words does the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms begin?
questions.a: Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law
w: We the people of Canada, in order to form a more perfect union
All Canadians are born free and equal in dignity
Peace, order and good government for all
questions.e: The Charter begins with the words: 'Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.'

questions.q: Which of these is a fundamental freedom protected in Canada?
questions.a: Freedom of conscience and religion
questions.e: Fundamental freedoms include freedom of conscience and religion; freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression; freedom of peaceful assembly; and freedom of association.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a fundamental freedom in Canada?
questions.a: Freedom to use violence to defend your opinions
w: Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression
questions.e: Canadians have freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, peaceful assembly and association. Using violence is against the law.

questions.q: Freedom of speech and freedom of the press are part of the fundamental freedoms in Canada.
questions.e: Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression includes freedom of speech and of the press.

questions.q: What do Mobility Rights in the Charter mean?
questions.a: Canadians can live and work anywhere in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport
w: Canadians must live in the province where they were born
Canadians need a permit to move to another province
Only citizens born in Canada can apply for a passport
questions.e: Mobility Rights: Canadians can live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely, and apply for a passport.

questions.q: Which of these is part of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
questions.a: Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights
w: The right to free university education
The right to own a car
The right to choose your own taxes
questions.e: The Charter includes Mobility Rights, Aboriginal Peoples' Rights, Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights, and Multiculturalism.

questions.q: The rights guaranteed in the Charter do not affect the treaty rights or other rights of Aboriginal peoples.
questions.e: Aboriginal Peoples' Rights: the rights in the Charter will not adversely affect any treaty or other rights or freedoms of Aboriginal peoples.

questions.q: Which Charter right says English and French have equal status in the Parliament and throughout the Government of Canada?
questions.a: Official Language Rights
questions.e: Under Official Language Rights, French and English have equal status in Parliament and throughout the federal government.

questions.q: What is multiculturalism in Canada?
questions.a: A fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage and identity
w: A law that says everyone must speak French
A rule that only allows immigrants from some countries
questions.e: Multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of Canadian heritage and identity. Canadians celebrate the gift of one another's presence and work hard to respect pluralism.

questions.q: Which old English document from 1215 is part of the history of our rights and freedoms?
questions.a: Magna Carta
questions.e: Canadian rights come from a tradition that includes Magna Carta, the Great Charter of Freedoms, signed in England in 1215.

questions.q: What is another name for Magna Carta?
questions.a: The Great Charter of Freedoms
w: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms
questions.e: Magna Carta, signed in England in 1215, is also known as the Great Charter of Freedoms.

questions.q: What is habeas corpus?
questions.a: The right to challenge being held unlawfully by the state
w: The right to a free lawyer for any case
The right to vote in elections
questions.e: Habeas corpus is the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state. It comes from English common law.

questions.q: Habeas corpus comes from English common law.
questions.e: Habeas corpus, the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state, comes from English common law.

questions.q: Which of these is a source of Canadian law?
questions.a: Laws passed by Parliament and the provincial legislatures
questions.e: Canadian law comes from laws passed by Parliament and the provincial legislatures, English common law, the civil code of France and the unwritten constitution inherited from Great Britain.

questions.q: The civil code of France is one of the sources of law in Canada.
questions.e: Canada's legal traditions include English common law and the civil code of France, which is used in Quebec for civil matters.

questions.q: Under Canadian law, how are men and women treated?
questions.a: Men and women are equal
w: Men have more rights than women
questions.e: In Canada, men and women are equal under the law.

questions.q: In Canada, spousal abuse, honour killings, female genital mutilation and forced marriage are crimes and are not tolerated.
questions.e: Canada's openness does not extend to barbaric cultural practices that tolerate spousal abuse, honour killings, female genital mutilation, forced marriage or other gender-based violence. These are severely punished under Canada's criminal laws.

questions.q: In Canada, a husband may legally use violence against his wife if it is part of his culture.
questions.e: Spousal abuse and other gender-based violence are crimes in Canada and are severely punished. Men and women are equal under the law.

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility of Canadian citizenship?
questions.a: Obeying the law
questions.e: Citizenship responsibilities include obeying the law, taking responsibility for yourself and your family, serving on a jury, voting, helping others in the community, and protecting our heritage and environment.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a responsibility of Canadian citizenship?
questions.a: Joining the Canadian Armed Forces
w: Serving on a jury when asked
questions.e: There is no compulsory military service in Canada. Serving is a noble choice, but it is not a citizenship responsibility.

questions.q: Which responsibility means every person, including judges, politicians and the police, must follow Canada's laws?
questions.a: Obeying the law
questions.e: One of Canada's founding principles is the rule of law. Individuals and governments are regulated by laws, not by arbitrary actions. No one is above the law.

questions.q: What does 'taking responsibility for oneself and one's family' mean?
questions.a: Getting a job, taking care of your family and working hard in keeping with your abilities
w: Asking the government to pay for everything
Letting your family make your decisions for you
Only working when you feel like it
questions.e: Getting a job, taking care of one's family and working hard in keeping with one's abilities are important Canadian values. Work contributes to personal dignity and self-respect.

questions.q: If you are called to serve on a jury, you are legally required to do so.
questions.e: Serving on a jury is a privilege that makes the justice system work. It is a legal requirement when you are called.

questions.q: Why is serving on a jury important?
questions.a: It helps make the justice system work, because it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens
w: It is a way to earn extra money
It lets you choose the punishment for any crime
It is only for lawyers and judges
questions.e: Serving on a jury is a privilege. The justice system depends on impartial juries made up of citizens.

questions.q: Voting in elections is described as what?
questions.a: Both a right and a responsibility
w: A right only for people born in Canada
A responsibility only for property owners
Neither a right nor a responsibility
questions.e: The right to vote comes with a responsibility to vote in federal, provincial or territorial and local elections.

questions.q: Which of these is a way of helping others in the community?
questions.a: Volunteering
questions.e: Millions of volunteers freely donate their time to help others. Volunteering is an excellent way to gain useful skills and develop friends and contacts.

questions.q: Which is an example of protecting and enjoying our heritage and environment?
questions.a: Avoiding littering and wasting resources
questions.e: Every citizen has a role in avoiding waste and pollution while protecting Canada's natural, cultural and architectural heritage for future generations.

questions.q: Getting a job and taking care of your family are important Canadian values.
questions.e: Working hard in keeping with your abilities and taking care of your family contribute to personal dignity, self-respect and the prosperity of Canada.

questions.q: There is compulsory military service in Canada.
questions.e: There is no compulsory military service in Canada. However, serving in the regular Canadian Forces (navy, army and air force) is a noble way to contribute to Canada.

questions.q: Which of these is a way to serve Canada?
questions.a: Joining the navy, army or air force, the Coast Guard, or the police or fire services
questions.e: Serving in the Canadian Forces is a noble way to contribute. You can also serve in the Coast Guard, police, fire service or the reserves, and young people can join cadets.

questions.q: What can young people join to learn about discipline, responsibility and skills?
questions.a: Cadets
questions.e: Young people can learn discipline, responsibility and skills by joining the cadets.

questions.q: In the Oath of Citizenship, new citizens promise to be faithful and bear true allegiance to whom?
questions.a: The King of Canada, King Charles III
questions.e: New citizens swear allegiance to the Sovereign, King Charles III, King of Canada. Older copies of Discover Canada name Queen Elizabeth II, who reigned until 2022.

questions.q: Since 2021, the Oath of Citizenship also includes a promise to observe the laws of Canada, including the Constitution, which recognizes and affirms whose rights?
questions.a: The Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples
w: The rights of members of Parliament
The rights of Canadians living abroad
questions.e: In 2021 the oath was changed to recognize and affirm the Aboriginal and treaty rights of First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples. Older copies of the guide show the earlier oath.

questions.q: In the Oath of Citizenship, you promise to fulfil your duties as a Canadian citizen.
questions.e: The oath ends with a promise to faithfully observe the laws of Canada and fulfil your duties as a Canadian citizen.

questions.q: What is the final step in becoming a Canadian citizen?
questions.a: Taking the Oath of Citizenship at a citizenship ceremony
questions.e: New citizens take the Oath of Citizenship at a citizenship ceremony. By doing so, they make a promise to Canada.

questions.q: Who must take the citizenship test?
questions.a: Applicants aged 18 to 54
w: Only applicants born outside the Commonwealth
questions.e: Applicants aged 18 to 54 must take the citizenship test and show they have adequate knowledge of English or French.

questions.q: Canadian citizenship was first created by law in which year?
questions.e: The first Canadian Citizenship Act came into force in 1947. Before that, people in Canada were British subjects.

questions.q: Canadian citizens have rights and responsibilities.
questions.e: Canadian citizens have rights and responsibilities that come from our history, are secured by Canadian law and reflect our shared traditions, identity and values.

questions.q: What does Canadian citizenship give you that a permanent resident does not have?
questions.a: The right to vote and to be a candidate in elections
w: The right to work in Canada
The right to free health care
The right to go to school
questions.e: Democratic Rights in the Charter, such as the right to vote and to be a candidate in elections, belong to Canadian citizens.

questions.q: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of the Constitution in 1867.
questions.e: The Charter was added to the Constitution in 1982. Confederation was in 1867.

questions.q: Mobility Rights mean Canadians need government permission to move to another province.
questions.e: Mobility Rights mean Canadians can live and work anywhere in Canada, and enter and leave the country freely.

questions.q: Voting in elections is a right but not a responsibility of Canadian citizens.
questions.e: Voting is both a right and a responsibility of citizenship.

questions.q: You can refuse to serve on a jury for any reason if you are called.
questions.e: Serving on a jury is a legal requirement when you are called. Only some people are excused for special reasons.

questions.q: Canadian citizens must give up all their old customs and traditions.
questions.e: Canadians are free to keep their cultural traditions, as long as they respect Canadian laws and values.
